candidates.question: A read-only report runs several SELECT statements in one explicit SQL Server 2022 transaction. Each must use one consistent transaction-level versioned view while other sessions can commit ordinary row updates between the report's reads. RCSI and ALLOW_SNAPSHOT_ISOLATION are enabled. There is no DDL or special locking hint. Which session isolation level meets both requirements?

answerChoices.text: READ COMMITTED under RCSI
SERIALIZABLE
SNAPSHOT
READ UNCOMMITTED

candidates.explanation: Use SNAPSHOT for the consistent transaction-level versioned view.
candidates.deepExplanation: RCSI changes READ COMMITTED at statement scope; SNAPSHOT changes the consistency scope to the transaction. The scenario deliberately excludes DDL/schema-lock contention and writer update-conflict handling.

whyOtherAnswersAreWrong.a: RCSI provides a fresh statement-level view. Separate statements can therefore observe different committed versions within the same transaction.
whyOtherAnswersAreWrong.b: Serializable isolation protects the read set with locks, so conflicting row updates cannot freely commit while those read locks are held.
whyOtherAnswersAreWrong.d: This level can expose uncommitted changes and does not establish the required stable committed transaction-level snapshot.

candidates.question: A SQL Server 2022 transaction uses SNAPSHOT to read a balance and calculate a debit. After that read, another transaction commits an update to the same row. The first transaction then attempts its UPDATE and encounters an update conflict. There are no external side effects, and bounded retries are permitted. Which response preserves the calculation's consistency?

answerChoices.text: Start a fresh transaction, reread the balance and re-evaluate the debit before retrying the complete operation.
Wait in the failed transaction until the other writer releases its lock, then reuse the calculated value.
Submit only the old calculated UPDATE value in a new transaction without rereading.
Treat the conflict as successful optimistic concurrency and commit the original debit.

candidates.explanation: Retry the complete read-calculate-write operation under a new transaction snapshot.
candidates.deepExplanation: SNAPSHOT stabilizes reads but does not silently authorize overwriting a concurrently changed row. This is a write-conflict decision, distinct from choosing transaction-level versus statement-level read consistency and from deadlock-victim selection.

whyOtherAnswersAreWrong.b: Waiting can resolve ordinary lock blocking while a transaction is still valid. Here the other writer has committed and the snapshot transaction has encountered a terminating update conflict.
whyOtherAnswersAreWrong.c: A new transaction could accept an update based on a fresh valid context, but reusing the old calculation skips the business decision against the now-current balance. It does not preserve the stated read-calculate-write consistency.
whyOtherAnswersAreWrong.d: A successful uncontested SNAPSHOT write can commit normally. An update conflict instead terminates the transaction; it is not evidence that the intended debit was accepted.

candidates.question: A SQL Server 2022 blocking snapshot shows UPDATE request 61 waiting on session 58, and UPDATE request 58 waiting on session 52. Session 52 is sleeping with one open transaction after an UPDATE and has no active request. An authorized operator must locate the transaction keeping this chain waiting. Which investigation should come first?

answerChoices.text: Inspect session 61's execution plan and test whether an index could reduce its lock footprint.
Inspect session 58's UPDATE predicate and test whether smaller batches could shorten its transaction.
Inspect system_health deadlock reports and plan recovery for a recorded victim.
Inspect session 52's open transaction and coordinate completion or rollback with its owning application.

candidates.explanation: Follow the waiting chain to session 52, then investigate its open transaction with the application owner.
candidates.deepExplanation: Session 58 is both a blocker and a waiter; the observed chain leads farther upstream to sleeping session 52. An active-request view does not establish that an idle session ended its transaction. Coordinate authorized completion or rollback rather than automatically issuing KILL or treating this live blocking chain as a rolled-back deadlock victim.

whyOtherAnswersAreWrong.a: Index analysis can help when a resource-intensive statement is the cause of long lock holding. Session 61 is a downstream waiter in this snapshot; tuning it does not first identify the upstream transaction keeping the chain blocked.
whyOtherAnswersAreWrong.b: Narrower predicates or batches can shorten a blocking transaction. Here session 58 is itself waiting on session 52, so starting with its workload misses the upstream open transaction.
whyOtherAnswersAreWrong.c: SQL Server's system_health session records deadlocks, and victim recovery is appropriate for a captured deadlock incident. The supplied waiting chain instead leads to a still-open sleeping transaction; a historical victim report is not the first investigation of that transaction.
